lessons.title: Introduction to HTML
lessons.content: HTML, or HyperText Markup Language, is the foundation of web pages. It uses tags to structure content like headings, paragraphs, and images.

lessons.title: Basic HTML Structure
lessons.content: Every HTML page starts with a <!DOCTYPE html> declaration, followed by an <html> tag containing <head> for metadata and <body> for visible content.

lessons.content: The tag creates a hyperlink. Use the href attribute to specify the URL, like Click me.

To create a link, use the <a> tag with an href attribute and add text between the opening and closing tags.

lessons.title: What Are HTML Lists?
lessons.content: HTML lists organize content in a structured way. Use <ul> for unordered (bulleted) lists and <ol> for ordered (numbered) lists, with <li> for each item.

lessons.title: Text Formatting
lessons.content: HTML provides tags like <strong> for bold text and <em> for italic text to emphasize content.

lessons.title: Which tag is used for an unordered list?
To create an unordered list, use the <ul> tag and wrap each item in <li> tags.
To emphasize text as italic, wrap it with the tag, like Italic text.

lessons.instruction: To create an ordered list, use the <ol> tag and wrap each item in <li> tags.

lessons.title: You’re Killing It! 🎉
lessons.content: Amazing work completing the HTML Lists and Formatting module! 🎊 You’re mastering the art of structuring web content. Let’s jump into the next challenge and keep the momentum going! 🚀

lessons.title: Introduction to HTML Tables
lessons.content: HTML tables organize data in rows and columns using the <table>, <tr> (row), and <td> (data cell) tags.

lessons.title: Using Attributes
lessons.content: Attributes provide extra information to tags. For example, the id attribute gives an element a unique identifier, like <div id='main'>.

lessons.title: Which tag defines a table row?
To create a table with one cell, use the <table>, <tr>, and <td> tags in that order.

To add an id attribute to a paragraph, include id='value' inside the opening

tag.

lessons.instruction: To create a table header, use the <th> tag inside a <tr> within a <table>.

lessons.question: Which attribute gives an element a unique identifier?
Which tag is used for a table data cell?

lessons.title: Way to Go! 🎉
lessons.content: You've aced the HTML Tables and Attributes module! 🎈 Your ability to structure data is top-notch. Let’s tackle the next challenge and keep building your web skills! 🚀

lessons.title: Introduction to HTML Forms
lessons.content: Forms allow users to input data. They're created with the <form> tag and can contain various input elements like text fields, checkboxes, and buttons.

lessons.title: Common Input Types
lessons.content: Use <input> with different type attributes: text (for regular text), password (hidden text), checkbox (toggle), and submit (form submission button).

lessons.title: Which tag is used to create a form?
To create a text input field, use <input type='text'> inside a form.
To create a submit button, use <input type='submit'> with an optional value attribute for the button text.

lessons.instruction: To create a password field, use <input type='password'> inside a form.

lessons.question: Which input type creates a checkbox?
What attribute specifies what text appears on a submit button?

lessons.title: Form Master Achieved! 🎉
lessons.content: You've successfully completed the HTML Forms module! 🎊 Now you can create interactive forms that collect user input. Your web skills are becoming more powerful with each lesson! 🚀

lessons.title: What Are Semantic Elements?
lessons.content: Semantic elements clearly describe their meaning to browsers and developers. Examples include <header>, <footer>, <article>, and <section>.

lessons.title: Common Semantic Tags
lessons.content: <header> defines introductory content, <nav> for navigation links, <main> for the main content, and <footer> for closing content.

lessons.title: Which tag is typically used for navigation links?
To create a basic page structure, use <header>, <main>, and <footer> tags in order.
To mark up an independent article, wrap your content in <article> tags.

lessons.instruction: To define a section in a document, use the <section> tag.

lessons.question: Which tag represents the main content of a document?
What is the advantage of semantic elements?

lessons.title: Semantic Pro! 🎉
lessons.content: Brilliant work on the HTML5 Semantic Elements module! 🎈 You now understand how to create meaningful page structures. Keep up the great work as we move forward! 🚀

lessons.title: Understanding Meta Tags
lessons.content: Meta tags in the <head> section provide metadata like character sets, page descriptions, and viewport settings that browsers and search engines use.

lessons.title: Essential Meta Tags
lessons.content: <meta charset='UTF-8'> sets character encoding, <meta name='viewport'> controls mobile display, and <meta name='description'> helps SEO.

lessons.title: Where do meta tags belong?
options: At the end of the file

lessons.title: The HTML Skeleton
lessons.content: Every HTML page needs this structure: <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head>, and <body> tags. The <head> contains invisible info, <body> has visible content.

lessons.title: The Title Tag
lessons.content: <title> in the <head> sets what appears in browser tabs. Example: <title>My Page</title> makes the tab show 'My Page'.

lessons.title: Headings Hierarchy
lessons.content: <h1> to <h6> create headings. <h1> is biggest (most important), <h6> is smallest. Use them in order like a document outline.

lessons.title: Why Use Comments?
lessons.content: Comments <!-- like this --> are notes in code that browsers ignore. They help explain your code to other developers (or your future self!).

lessons.title: Comment Syntax
lessons.content: Comments start with <!-- and end with -->. They can span multiple lines. Example: <!-- Navigation starts here -->.

lessons.title: The Div Element
lessons.content: <div> is a container that groups elements together. It's like an invisible box to organize content or apply styles to multiple elements.

lessons.title: Why Use Divs?
lessons.content: Divs help structure pages. You can give them IDs (<div id='header'>) or classes (<div class='menu'>) to style them with CSS later.

lessons.content: <span> is an inline container for small text pieces. Unlike <div>, it doesn't create line breaks. Use it to style parts of text differently.
